BA-01.title: Role of the Business Analyst (vs Product/Project Manager)
BA-01.one_screen: A BA in a bank translates business needs into requirements, focusing on *what* and *why*, unlike a product manager (who defines product strategy and features) or a project manager (who plans the *how* and *when* of delivery).

BA-02.title: Change Landscape: Regulatory vs Strategic vs Remediation
BA-02.one_screen: Banks undertake strategic initiatives (growth or efficiency) and remediation (fixing defects), but *regulatory-driven* change is mandatory, with fixed deadlines and external oversight, requiring full compliance and auditability.

Ramki Ravulapalli – “Regulatory Projects” (waterfall, deadlines)

BA-03.title: Stakeholders in Bank Change Programs
BA-03.one_screen: Successful change requires early and ongoing involvement of all impacted groups: business owners (front-line and process managers), risk and compliance, finance, IT/operations, data/model owners, internal audit and (where needed) the regulator.

BA-04.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
BA-04.one_screen: Elicitation is gathering information on what stakeholders need.  Techniques include structured interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, surveys, and prototyping, chosen based on context and participant availability.

Bridging the Gap – Eliciting from Busy Stakeholders (importance of agenda, homework)

BA-05.title: Interviewing Time-Pressed Subject Matter Experts
BA-05.one_screen: SMEs are often busy and short on time.  Always prepare an agenda and pre-reads, ask targeted questions, and build credibility so even a short meeting is productive.

sources.label: Bridging the Gap – “Interviewing a Subject Matter Expert” (be prepared, agenda)

BA-06.title: Process Mapping (As-Is vs To-Be)
BA-06.one_screen: Process mapping diagrams the workflow of a process.  Mapping the current “as-is” process clarifies existing steps and bottlenecks; the “to-be” map lays out the improved future workflow.  Visualizing both highlights where changes are needed.

sources.label: IBM Blueprint (IBM KB) – “A process map outlines steps... reveals areas of improvement”
IBM – definition of process mapping for clarity

BA-07.title: Root Cause Analysis
BA-07.one_screen: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a method to find the underlying cause of a problem or error, not just its symptoms.  Techniques like “5 Whys” and fishbone diagrams are used to dig down to the true source of an issue.

sources.label: BA Times – “Root Cause Analysis is a method of identifying the underlying cause of a problem... using cause-and-effect diagrams, flowcharts, etc.”

BA-08.title: Requirements Traceability (Matrix)
BA-08.one_screen: A traceability matrix links each requirement through design, code and testing.  It ensures every requirement (especially regulatory ones) is accounted for and verified.  This audit trail of requirements-to-tests is vital for regulators and audits.

sources.label: Visure Solutions – “Traceability Matrix... traces and maps requirements to project artifacts... gives a clear audit trail to demonstrate compliance”

BA-09.title: Business Requirements Document (BRD)
BA-09.one_screen: The BRD captures *what* the business wants and *why*, including objectives, scope, stakeholders, and high-level requirements. It **must not** include solution design or technical details. Each requirement should have acceptance criteria.

sources.label: Monday.com – capturing requirements with acceptance criteria

BA-10.title: Functional Specifications vs Business Requirements
BA-10.one_screen: **Business requirements** state *what* is needed, while **functional specifications** describe *how* the system will meet those needs.  A business requirement is high-level (e.g. “produce regulatory report X”), whereas a functional spec details the software logic, screens, or data elements to implement it. The BRD avoids technical detail.

sources.label: Monday.com – “no excessive technical detail” in BRD template

BA-11.title: Data Mapping Specification
BA-11.one_screen: A data mapping spec is a field-by-field table linking each source field to a target field, including data type and the transformation rule.  It documents exactly how data moves or is converted from the old system to the new.

sources.label: BA Careers – Definition of data mapping and example mapping table

BA-12.title: Non-Functional Requirements (Performance, Retention, Auditability)
BA-12.one_screen: Non-functional requirements define *how* the system performs: its quality attributes like speed, security, data retention, and audit capabilities. In banking, **auditability** (e.g. full logging and data retention) is often mandated for compliance.

sources.label: LinkedIn (Rosmary Okordion) – banking NFRs including Auditability requirement

BA-13.title: Testable Acceptance Criteria
BA-13.one_screen: Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions that define when a requirement is met.  Well-crafted criteria are clear, concise, and objectively verifiable.

Atlassian – acceptance criteria must be “objectively verifiable”

BA-14.title: User Stories and Acceptance in a Regulated Context
BA-14.one_screen: In agile development, user stories (“As a user, I want…”) drive increments.  In a regulated project, each story’s acceptance criteria must tie back to formal requirements and evidence.  You may still use stories, but supplement them with thorough documentation and approvals for audit purposes.

BA-15.title: Testing Lifecycle (Unit, System, Integration, UAT)
BA-15.one_screen: A typical banking IT change goes through multiple test phases: Unit testing (by developers), Integration/System testing (by QA/IT), and User Acceptance Testing (by business).  Each phase has different owners and objectives.

sources.label: Yethi Consulting – Core banking UAT (business-led)

BA-16.title: Test Planning and Test Packs
BA-16.one_screen: A test plan defines the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of testing. Test packs (test cases and data) list the specific scenarios with expected outcomes.  For each requirement, predefined test cases and datasets must be prepared before testing begins.

BA-17.title: UAT Coverage and Defect Management
BA-17.one_screen: Ensure UAT covers all critical business and regulatory scenarios. Use metrics (e.g. scenario coverage %) to argue sufficiency.  Manage defects by classifying each by *severity* (technical impact) and *priority* (business urgency).

BA-18.title: Parallel Running & Go-Live Planning
BA-18.one_screen: *Parallel running* means operating the old and new systems side-by-side for a period to compare outputs. *Go-live planning* (cutover) details how to switch to the new system, including rollback steps if needed.  Both are critical in regulated transitions.

sources.label: OCM Solution – “Cutover and rollback steps” in go-live checklist

BA-19.title: Post-Implementation Review and Benefits Realisation
BA-19.one_screen: After go-live, conduct a formal review comparing actual outcomes to planned objectives. Capture lessons learned and track whether expected benefits (cost savings, efficiency gains, compliance) are realized.

sources.label: Project Delivery (UK government) – benefits management and review principles (general reference)

BA-20.title: Waterfall vs Agile in Banking
BA-20.one_screen: Waterfall (stage-gate) and Agile (iterative) are both used in banks.  Regulatory changes often lean waterfall: fixed scope and deadlines drive sequential phases (requirements→design→build→test). Agile is better for evolving requirements, but must be adapted for compliance needs.

sources.label: Ramki Ravulapalli – “Banks deal with regulatory initiatives by setting up Waterfall style... finalise requirements, then design, then build and test”

BA-21.title: Prioritisation & Estimation in Banking Projects
BA-21.one_screen: Prioritize work using clear criteria (business value, risk, regulatory urgency) and defend choices with data.  Estimate tasks realistically using ranges or past data, accounting for optimism bias.

BA-22.title: Managing Scope Change with Fixed Deadlines
BA-22.one_screen: In projects with immovable regulatory deadlines, handle scope changes through a formal change control process.  Assess each new requirement’s impact on timeline and scope. If the deadline cannot move, negotiate resources or de-scope non-critical items rather than slipping the date.

CAP-01.title: Why Regulatory Capital Exists
CAP-01.one_screen: Expected loss is the centre of a loss distribution; unexpected loss is the adverse loss beyond that centre. IMP-01 → a loss allowance reduces an asset's carrying amount, while capital is loss-absorbing resource against unexpected loss. Regulatory capital exists to preserve solvency when realised losses outrun earnings and recognised loss allowances.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Modifications to the capital treatment for expected and unexpected credit losses*, BCBS 104, 30 January 2004.

CAP-02.title: Loss Absorption: Going Concern to Resolution
CAP-02.one_screen: FND-04 → capital is not liquidity: capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets payments when due. Within capital itself, timing matters: going-concern resources absorb loss while the bank remains viable, while gone-concern resources support creditor protection and resolution after viability is lost.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*, CAP10, last update 5 June 2020.

CAP-03.title: The Capital Quality Hierarchy
CAP-03.one_screen: Regulatory capital is nested by quality. CET1 is the highest-quality layer; CET1 plus AT1 is Tier 1; Tier 1 plus Tier 2 is Total Capital. Because the categories are nested, lower-quality capital cannot repair a shortfall in a higher-quality requirement.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*, CAP10, last update 5 June 2020.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*, RBC20, last update 26 November 2020, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-04.title: Common Equity Tier 1
CAP-04.one_screen: CET1 is the highest-quality regulatory capital because it bears losses continuously and is not protected by a contractual promise of repayment. FND-03 → retained earnings accumulate profit after distributions; losses run through earnings and therefore reduce CET1 unless another qualifying capital action offsets them.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*, CAP10, last update 5 June 2020.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP30 — Regulatory adjustments*, CAP30, published 15 December 2019.

CAP-05.title: Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2
CAP-05.one_screen: AT1 and Tier 2 extend loss-bearing capacity beyond common equity, but they do so with lower regulatory quality. AT1 remains within going-concern Tier 1; Tier 2 is principally the gone-concern layer. Neither category exists merely because a security is marketed as a hybrid or subordinated bond.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*, CAP10, last update 5 June 2020.

Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP20 — Minority interest and other capital issued out of consolidated subsidiaries that is held by third parties*, CAP20, published 15 December 2019.

CAP-06.title: From Accounting Equity to Regulatory Capital
CAP-06.one_screen: Accounting equity answers a reporting question; regulatory CET1 answers whether an amount is sufficiently reliable and available to absorb prudential loss. Regulatory adjustments therefore remove, filter or limit items that could disappear in stress, create double counting or produce capital that is not economically available to the banking group.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP30 — Regulatory adjustments*, CAP30, published 15 December 2019.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*, CAP10, last update 5 June 2020.

CAP-07.title: Where Allowances Meet Capital
CAP-07.one_screen: IMP-01 owns the object distinction: allowance is a reduction in an asset's carrying amount; capital is loss-absorbing resource. This atom owns the transmission between them. A higher credit-loss allowance reduces earnings or opening retained earnings, which usually reduces CET1; prudential rules can then make further capital adjustments without turning the allowance itself into capital.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP30 — Regulatory adjustments*, CAP30, published 15 December 2019.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE35 — IRB approach: treatment of expected losses and provisions*, CRE35, published 27 March 2020, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-08.title: Regulatory Expected Loss and Eligible Provisions
CAP-08.one_screen: CR-09 → expected loss is a governed PD/LGD/EAD quantity; IMP-01 → an accounting allowance is not capital. Under IRB, Basel nevertheless compares regulatory expected loss with eligible provisions so expected credit loss is not silently left uncovered or double-counted in the capital stack.

CAP-09.title: ECL Transition and Regulatory Capital Relief
CAP-09.one_screen: A new ECL regime can create an immediate opening-equity hit before the underlying loans have changed overnight. Transitional capital relief smooths that prudential shock; it does not undo the allowance. **As at August 2026**, RBI's final ECL Directions are issued but not yet in force: they commence on **1 April 2027** and permit a declining CET1 add-back through **31 March 2031**.

CAP-10.title: Capital Ratio Anatomy
CAP-10.one_screen: A capital ratio combines two governed quantities: qualifying capital in the numerator and risk-weighted assets in the denominator. A bank can lose capital adequacy because the numerator falls, because RWA rises, or because both move against it at the same time.

CAP-11.title: Risk Weights and Risk-Weighted Assets
CAP-11.one_screen: FND-11 → exposure is the amount at risk under a defined measurement basis. A risk weight scales that exposure into regulatory RWA; it is not a forecast of the percentage that will default or be lost.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE20 — Standardised approach: individual exposures*, CRE20, last update 10 June 2025, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-12.title: The RWA Engines
CAP-12.one_screen: Total RWA is not produced by one universal risk-weight formula. Separate prudential engines measure credit, market, operational and CVA-related risks under their own rules, then feed a common risk-based capital denominator.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*, RBC20, last update 26 November 2020, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-13.title: Standardised Credit Risk: Exposure to RWA
CAP-13.one_screen: CR-01/02 → obligor and facility are different risk objects. Under the standardised approach, the prudential rulebook classifies the exposure, determines the regulatory exposure amount and applies prescribed risk drivers and weights rather than allowing the bank's own PD/LGD model to generate the core capital requirement.

CAP-14.title: Credit Risk Mitigation: Recognition Before Relief
CAP-14.one_screen: CR-07 → collateral mitigates loss severity; it does not replace repayment capacity. Regulatory capital goes one step further: economic protection reduces RWA only when the protection is eligible, legally effective and recognised by the applicable prudential method.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE22 — Standardised approach: credit risk mitigation*, CRE22, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-15.title: CRM Mechanics: Substitution, Netting and Haircuts
CAP-15.one_screen: Once protection passes the eligibility gate, the capital calculation must use the right mechanism. Guarantees typically change whose credit quality drives the protected portion; collateral changes recognised exposure value; netting recognises enforceable offsets. Haircuts protect the calculation against value movement before close-out or realisation.

CAP-16.title: IRB: Permission, Scope and Architecture
CAP-16.one_screen: CR-04/05/06 → PD, LGD and EAD are governed risk parameters. IRB allows an approved bank to estimate specified inputs for regulatory capital, but Basel still controls the asset classes, minimum requirements, parameter definitions and risk-weight functions. Internal modelling is permissioned prudential machinery, not a bank-selected alternative formula.

CAP-17.title: The IRB Risk Function
CAP-17.one_screen: CR-04/05/06 → PD, LGD and EAD measure different dimensions of credit loss; CR-10 → point-in-time and through-the-cycle calibration are not interchangeable. The IRB function combines regulatory parameters with supervisory maturity and correlation relationships to target unexpected portfolio loss, not merely expected loss.

CAP-18.title: IRB Constraints and Specialised Lending
CAP-18.one_screen: Internal estimates are not allowed to fall without limit or to be used for every exposure. Basel constrains IRB through parameter floors, minimum data and estimation rules, exposure-class restrictions and, for qualifying specialised lending, a supervisory slotting route that classifies transaction quality rather than relying on an ordinary corporate PD/LGD treatment.

CAP-19.title: The Output Floor
CAP-19.one_screen: The output floor limits how far approved internal models can reduce aggregate RWA below a standardised benchmark. The fully phased Basel calibration is 72.5% of standardised RWA; it is not a 72.5% exposure risk weight. **As at August 2026**, phase-in status is jurisdiction-specific and future steps must be read by date.

CAP-20.title: The Leverage Ratio Backstop
CAP-20.one_screen: Risk-based capital asks how risky exposures are; the leverage ratio asks how large the bank's exposure is relative to Tier 1 capital without ordinary credit risk weighting. Basel deliberately uses it as a simple non-risk-based backstop against model risk, classification risk and excessive balance-sheet leverage.

CAP-21.title: Three Pillars, One Capital Architecture
CAP-21.one_screen: The three Basel pillars answer different questions. Pillar 1 asks what prescribed quantitative minimum follows from the rulebook; Pillar 2 asks what material risk and vulnerability that minimum does not fully capture; Pillar 3 asks what must be disclosed so outsiders can assess the prudential position. Buffers are not a fourth pillar: they sit above capital requirements.

CAP-22.title: Pillar 1: Minimum Risk-Based Capital
CAP-22.one_screen: Pillar 1 converts prescribed risk measurement into minimum capital requirements. It is deliberately standardised enough to be comparable across banks, but it is not intended to describe every risk that could threaten a particular institution.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*, RBC20, last update 26 November 2020, effective 1 January 2023.

CAP-23.title: Pillar 2: ICAAP, Supervisory Review and Add-ons
CAP-23.one_screen: Pillar 2 is the completeness check on Pillar 1. ICAAP is management's disciplined argument that the bank's capital is adequate for its actual risk profile and strategy; supervisory review independently tests that argument and can require remediation or capital above the minimum.

CAP-24.title: The Buffer Stack
CAP-24.one_screen: Buffers answer a different question from minimum requirements: how much CET1 should remain available above requirements so the bank can absorb stress before breaching the prudential floor? Conservation, countercyclical and systemic buffers have different triggers and purposes, even when they all add CET1.

CAP-25.title: Using the Stack: Distribution Constraints and Headroom
CAP-25.one_screen: Regulatory buffers are designed to be usable, but using them is not consequence-free. As CET1 falls from management headroom into regulatory buffers, restrictions on dividends, variable remuneration and other distributions conserve capital before minimum requirements are breached.

CAP-26.title: Stress Testing and Capital Transmission
CAP-26.one_screen: A capital stress test is a causal model, not a haircut applied to today's ratio. Scenario shocks change defaults, market values, revenues, expenses and balance-sheet behaviour; those changes affect both capital resources and RWA before the stressed ratio is recalculated.

CAP-27.title: Basel Standard to Binding Rule
CAP-27.one_screen: Basel is an international prudential standard, not a supranational banking statute. **As at August 2026**, the Basel Committee continues to set the common benchmark, while binding obligations arise through national or regional implementation. Every live capital question must therefore be dated and scoped before the formula is applied.

CR-01.title: Obligor, borrower and counterparty
CR-01.one_screen: Credit risk attaches to a person that owes performance, not to a customer label. **Obligor** identifies the legal or natural person responsible for the credit obligation; **borrower** and **counterparty** describe roles that may coincide with the obligor but need not.

CR-02.title: Product, facility and account
CR-02.one_screen: A product is a reusable lending design, a facility is a specific contractual grant of credit, and an account is an operational record used to book and service activity. Credit risk measures become ambiguous unless they declare which level they attach to.

CR-03.title: Exposure and aggregation levels
CR-03.one_screen: Exposure is the amount or value subject to credit loss for a stated purpose; it is not automatically today’s drawn balance. The same relationship can produce different valid exposure numbers at account, facility, obligor, connected-group and portfolio levels.

CR-04.title: Connected counterparties and economic groups
CR-04.one_screen: Legal separation does not guarantee independent credit risk. Connected-counterparty analysis aggregates persons when control or economic interdependence creates a common failure channel, so one concentrated risk cannot be disguised as several names.

CR-05.title: Underwriting and the credit decision
CR-05.one_screen: Underwriting converts information about the obligor, facility and environment into a governed decision to approve, decline or reshape credit. The decision starts with a sustainable **primary source of repayment**; collateral and guarantees can reduce loss if repayment fails, but they do not repair weak repayment capacity.

CR-06.title: Collateral, security and guarantees
CR-06.one_screen: Collateral, security interests and guarantees are credit-risk mitigants only to the extent that the bank can legally rely on them and realise value when needed. Their underwriting job is to provide a credible **secondary way out**; their later LGD role is separate and depends on realised recovery cash flows.

CR-07.title: Default: defining the event
CR-07.one_screen: Default is a governed credit state, not a synonym for arrears, loss, bankruptcy or write-off. Every PD, default rate, cure rate and LGD inherits the unit and events used in the default definition, so the event must be fixed before the metric.

CR-08.one_screen: Arrears measure unpaid contractual amounts; days past due measure how long payment has remained unpaid; delinquency buckets convert that clock into operational states. These are payment facts, not loss estimates or the complete definition of default.

CR-09.title: Unlikeliness to pay
CR-09.one_screen: Unlikeliness to pay identifies default from the substance of credit deterioration before a delinquency clock necessarily reaches its backstop. CR-10.one_screen: A past-due backstop is an outer mechanical trigger, not permission to wait for the clock when earlier evidence already establishes default. In the Basel wholesale reference definition, UTP and more-than-90-days-past-due are joined by **OR**, not by a sequence requiring both.

CR-11.one_screen: Restructuring changes contractual terms; forbearance is a concession associated with the debtor’s financial difficulty. A modification can preserve value, but cannot erase the deterioration that made the original terms unsustainable.

CR-12.title: Cure, probation and re-default
CR-12.one_screen: Cure is the governed transition from default back to non-default after the default conditions have ceased and renewed performance is credible. Re-default is a later return to default; a temporary payment or zero-DPD snapshot is not enough to prove a durable cure.

CR-13.title: Write-off, recovery and economic loss
CR-13.one_screen: Write-off changes the carrying amount or prudential treatment of an exposure; recovery records value collected after credit failure; economic loss measures what was ultimately lost after recoveries, costs and timing. None of these events should erase the default lifecycle that produced them.

CR-14.title: Probability of default
CR-14.one_screen: Probability of default is the probability that a defined obligor, facility or pool enters a defined default state over a specified future horizon, conditional on information available at an observation date. A number labelled “PD” is incomplete until its **unit, event, horizon and conditioning information** are known.

CR-15.title: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle PD
CR-15.one_screen: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle describe how strongly a rating or PD responds to current versus cyclical conditions. They are conditioning philosophies on a spectrum, not synonyms for short-horizon and long-horizon probability.

CR-16.title: Loss given default and recovery rate
CR-16.one_screen: Loss given default is loss severity **conditional on default**. Collateral and guarantees influence LGD only through legally available, economically realised recovery value; an appraisal at origination is therefore an input to recovery expectations, not the LGD itself.

CR-17.title: Exposure at default and credit conversion factors
CR-17.one_screen: Exposure at default estimates or prescribes how much is exposed when default occurs, not how much is drawn today. Credit conversion factors translate undrawn or contingent amounts into exposure, making pre-default utilisation behaviour part of credit risk.

CR-18.one_screen: `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` is a compact one-period loss decomposition only when the three inputs describe compatible default events, horizons, populations and economic conditions. The arithmetic is trivial; parameter alignment is the real mechanism.

CR-19.title: Retail versus wholesale credit modelling
CR-19.one_screen: Retail credit is usually managed through large pools of comparatively homogeneous exposures, making repeated statistical patterns powerful evidence. Wholesale credit is usually more obligor-centred because exposures are larger, populations are smaller and borrower-specific financial, structural and legal information matters more.

CR-20.title: Application, behavioural and bureau credit data
CR-20.one_screen: Application models use information available at or before origination; behavioural models use information generated after the relationship exists; bureau or credit-information data add externally reported indebtedness and repayment history. Their common discipline is **time**: only information genuinely available at the decision or observation date may enter the prediction.

CR-21.title: Rating grades, master scales and migration
CR-21.one_screen: A rating grade is a discrete class of borrower credit quality; a master scale defines the ordered meaning of all grades; migration records movement through that scale over time. A grade is not meaningful because it is called “4” or “BBB-like”—its meaning comes from assignment criteria, ordering, default boundary and calibrated risk.

CR-22.title: Vintage analysis and roll rates
CR-22.one_screen: Vintage analysis follows exposures originated at similar times as they season; roll-rate analysis follows movement between delinquency or credit states. Both restore the time dimension that a portfolio snapshot destroys.

sources.label: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, *Estimation Methodologies for Losses, Revenues, and Expenses*, August 2013

CR-23.title: Concentration and diversification
CR-23.one_screen: Concentration risk arises when too much exposure depends on the same name, connected group, sector, geography, collateral type or underlying economic driver. Diversification comes from genuinely different sources of loss, not from the number of rows, facilities or legal entities in a dataset.

CR-24.title: Correlation and systematic credit risk
CR-24.one_screen: Credit correlation means default and loss outcomes are not independent because common economic forces move many borrowers together. Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified across sufficiently independent exposures; systematic risk cannot be removed by adding more borrowers exposed to the same underlying conditions.

CR-25.title: Unexpected loss and capital
CR-25.one_screen: Expected loss is the average credit cost under a defined measurement; unexpected loss is adverse variation around that average. Capital protects solvency against sufficiently severe outcomes above ordinary expected-loss capacity, so portfolio dispersion and dependence matter even when exposure-level EL is unchanged.

CR-26.title: The credit-loss architecture
CR-26.one_screen: Credit risk is one continuous system: identify the person and exposure, decide whether repayment is sustainable, recognise default consistently, measure probability, severity and exposure, then aggregate common loss drivers into portfolio tail risk. The architecture fails when adjacent layers are collapsed—for example, collateral into repayment capacity, DPD into default, score into PD, or expected loss into capital.

DAT-01.title: Risk Data as an Enterprise Discipline
DAT-01.one_screen: Risk data management is the discipline of making risk information reliable enough to steer a bank, not merely storing data or producing reports. It connects governed source data to aggregation, decisions, internal risk reporting and supervisory reporting, with evidence that the chain can still work under stress.

DAT-02.title: BCBS 239: The Fourteen-Principle Architecture
DAT-02.one_screen: BCBS 239 is the Basel Committee's data aggregation and internal risk reporting standard, not a capital calculation rule. Its fourteen principles form one chain: governance and infrastructure enable reliable aggregation; reliable aggregation enables useful reporting; supervisors assess whether the whole capability works.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-03.title: BCBS 239 Governance and Data Architecture
DAT-03.one_screen: BCBS 239 Principles 1-2 make risk data a management-body and enterprise-architecture responsibility. The bank must be able to aggregate and report material risk information despite legal-entity complexity, organisational change, stress, acquisitions or fragmented technology.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-04.title: BCBS 239 Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities
DAT-04.one_screen: BCBS 239 Principles 3-6 define what a bank's aggregation engine must achieve: accurate and integral data, complete coverage, decision-useful timeliness and adaptability to new questions. The standard is outcomes-based; it does not create a universal 95 percent completeness threshold or a universal daily or intraday frequency.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-05.title: BCBS 239 Risk Reporting Practices
DAT-05.one_screen: BCBS 239 Principles 7-11 govern the report after aggregation: it must faithfully represent risk, cover the material picture, communicate it clearly, arrive at the right frequency and reach the right recipients. A technically correct dataset can still fail BCBS 239 if the report obscures the decision, omits relevant context or is distributed too late.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-06.title: BCBS 239 Supervisory Review and Implementation Record
DAT-06.one_screen: BCBS 239 does not end when a bank writes a policy: Principles 12-14 require supervisors to assess implementation, demand remediation and cooperate across home and host authorities. The implementation record remains active; a Basel Committee newsletter dated 6 January 2026 describes persistent challenges and expressly states that it creates no new supervisory guidance or expectations.

DAT-07.title: Golden Source and Authoritative Data
DAT-07.one_screen: A golden source is the governed authority for a defined data element or dataset, not simply the database with the newest copy. Authority means the bank has decided which source wins, for what scope and time, with ownership, controls and explicit treatment of downstream copies and exceptions.

DAT-08.title: Critical Data Elements
DAT-08.one_screen: Critical Data Elements, or CDEs, are data elements whose failure could materially impair risk management, financial or supervisory reporting, customer or business decisions, or regulatory compliance. CDE designation is a scoping mechanism: it concentrates stronger ownership, lineage, quality and change controls where failure matters most.

DAT-09.title: Data Owner, Steward, Producer, Consumer and Challenge
DAT-09.one_screen: Risk data governance fails when accountability is collapsed into one vague "data team". The owner, steward, producer, consumer and challenge function answer different questions: who is accountable for meaning and fitness, who operates governance, who creates or transforms the data, who relies on it, and who independently tests the evidence.

DAT-10.title: Data Governance Operating Models
DAT-10.one_screen: A data governance operating model turns roles into decision rights, forums, escalation paths and repeatable processes. Centralised, federated and hybrid models are organisational choices; none works if ownership is unclear or enterprise standards can be bypassed without controlled exception.

DAT-11.title: Business Lineage vs Technical Lineage
DAT-11.one_screen: Data lineage explains how a data item moves from origin to use and what happens to it on the way. Business lineage preserves meaning and dependency at a level a risk or reporting user can challenge; technical lineage preserves the physical systems, fields, transformations and interfaces needed to reproduce and troubleshoot the result.

sources.label: European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Implementation of the Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS Newsletter, 6 January 2026.

DAT-12.title: Metadata and the Business Glossary
DAT-12.one_screen: Metadata makes data interpretable and governable; a business glossary makes important business terms mean the same thing across functions and systems. Together they connect a human concept such as "counterparty exposure" to the fields, formats, owners, sources and lineage through which that concept is implemented.

sources.label: European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.
DAMA International, DAMA-DMBOK: Data Management Body of Knowledge, second edition, ISBN 9781634622486, 2017.

DAT-13.title: Master Data vs Reference Data
DAT-13.one_screen: Master data identifies and describes persistent business entities such as customers, counterparties, products or legal entities; reference data provides controlled code sets and classifications used to describe or group those entities and transactions. Both are shared across processes, but they solve different data problems and require different change controls.

sources.label: DAMA International, DAMA-DMBOK: Data Management Body of Knowledge, second edition, ISBN 9781634622486, 2017.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-14.title: Data Quality Dimensions
DAT-14.one_screen: Data quality is not one score. A dataset can be complete but inaccurate, valid but stale, or internally consistent while duplicating the same customer twice; quality must therefore be assessed across distinct dimensions against the needs of the specific risk or reporting use.

sources.label: European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.
DAMA International, DAMA-DMBOK: Data Management Body of Knowledge, second edition, ISBN 9781634622486, 2017.

DAT-15.title: Data Quality Rules, Thresholds and Monitoring
DAT-15.one_screen: A data-quality dimension becomes operational only when it is converted into a rule that can be executed, measured and escalated. A complete rule defines its population, condition, expected result, tolerance, ownership and breach action; a threshold without those elements is merely a number.

sources.label: European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-16.title: Reconciliation and Break Governance
DAT-16.one_screen: Reconciliation compares two governed populations or totals that should agree after known differences are understood. Its value is not the act of matching numbers; it is the disciplined classification, ownership, ageing and clearance of breaks so unexplained differences cannot quietly enter risk reports or returns.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-17.title: Data Issue Management and Remediation
DAT-17.one_screen: A data issue is not closed when the immediate report is patched. Controlled remediation separates containment from permanent correction, identifies the root cause, assigns accountable ownership, validates the fix and retains evidence that the defect no longer recurs or remains within an explicitly accepted risk position.

sources.label: European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Implementation of the Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS Newsletter, 6 January 2026.

DAT-18.title: Data Requirements and Acceptance Criteria
DAT-18.one_screen: A data requirement converts a regulatory, risk or business need into a statement precise enough to source, build and test. For a business analyst, the critical move is from "produce this field" to governed meaning, grain, population, timing, transformation, control and acceptance criteria that different teams can implement consistently.

European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-19.title: Source Discovery and ETL Sourcing Analysis
DAT-19.one_screen: Source discovery is the analysis required before a mapping can be trusted. The BA or data analyst identifies candidate sources, determines their grain, keys, history, authority, refresh, embedded transformations and quality limitations, then documents why the selected path is appropriate for the requirement.

sources.label: International Institute of Business Analysis, A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide Version 3, ISBN 9781927584026, 2015.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-20.title: Source-to-Target Mapping Specification
DAT-20.one_screen: A source-to-target mapping specification is the field-level implementation contract between a governed source and a target dataset, report or return. It must make joins, filters, transformations, classifications, defaults and lineage explicit enough that development and testing can independently reproduce the intended result.

sources.label: International Institute of Business Analysis, A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide Version 3, ISBN 9781927584026, 2015.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-21.title: Test Strategy and Test Packs
DAT-21.one_screen: Testing proves that approved requirements and mappings have been implemented, not merely that code executes without error. A test strategy defines what must be proven across the data chain; a test pack turns that strategy into traceable scenarios, inputs, expected outcomes and retained evidence.

sources.label: International Institute of Business Analysis, A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide Version 3, ISBN 9781927584026, 2015.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-22.title: UAT Coverage and Business Evidence
DAT-22.one_screen: User Acceptance Testing, or UAT, is the business decision that the delivered data behaviour satisfies the approved need in realistic use. It is not a duplicate of developer testing: UAT focuses on end-to-end business scenarios, definitions, usability, exceptions and evidence that the consumer can rely on the output.

sources.label: International Institute of Business Analysis, A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide Version 3, ISBN 9781927584026, 2015.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.

DAT-23.title: Downstream Extract Validation
DAT-23.one_screen: A change can be correct in the warehouse and still be wrong in the file actually consumed or submitted. Downstream extract validation proves that the final population, fields, totals, formats and cut-off survive every post-mapping transformation, aggregation and packaging step.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-24.title: Defect Tracking, Retest and Closure
DAT-24.one_screen: Delivery defects need a controlled lifecycle separate from long-term enterprise data issues, while material defects can escalate into that issue framework. A defect record links observed failure to requirement, mapping, severity, fix, retest and regression evidence so release decisions are based on known residual risk.

sources.label: International Institute of Business Analysis, A Guide to the Business Analysis Body of Knowledge, BABOK Guide Version 3, ISBN 9781927584026, 2015.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-25.title: Regulatory Returns Production Cycle
DAT-25.one_screen: A regulatory return is produced through a controlled recurring cycle, not a one-off query at filing time. The cycle freezes the applicable requirement and reference date, sources the governed population, transforms it into return fields, validates and reconciles the output, resolves exceptions and creates a submission-ready artifact with retained evidence.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, BCBS 239, 9 January 2013.
European Central Bank Banking Supervision, Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting, reference number not stated, 3 May 2024.

DAT-26.title: Submission, Attestation and Restatement
DAT-26.one_screen: Submission is the control boundary where a production-ready return becomes an official filing. Attestation or authorised sign-off establishes accountable approval where the applicable regime requires it; if a material error is discovered afterwards, the bank must assess the affected filing, follow the regulator's correction process and preserve a clear restatement trail.

DAT-27.title: EU COREP/FINREP and UK PRA Reporting
DAT-27.one_screen: EU and UK prudential reporting share historical roots but are now separate estates. EU institutions use EBA supervisory frameworks such as COREP and FINREP with the EBA Data Point Model and taxonomies; PRA firms use applicable UK data items and Bank of England taxonomies.

DAT-28.title: US Regulatory Reports
DAT-28.one_screen: US prudential reporting is organised around named form families with respondent panels and form-specific instructions rather than one COREP-style taxonomy estate. The bank must determine form applicability from institution profile and current instructions, then preserve mappings to each required schedule.

DAT-29.title: RBI Returns, ADF and CIMS
DAT-29.one_screen: India's supervisory reporting architecture combines return-specific RBI directions, the Automated Data Flow discipline and CIMS as a major filing platform. The durable objective is governed system-to-regulator flow with defined sources, reconciliation and increasing automation, while RBI's SDMX element-based programme remains an evolving architecture as at August 2026.

FND-01.title: Bank as a Balance Sheet
FND-01.one_screen: A bank is first an accounting entity with resources, obligations, and a residual claim. The identity **Assets = Liabilities + Equity** is the frame through which every later banking concept—lending, deposits, profit, capital, liquidity, and loss—must be read.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting*, revised March 2018, Chapters 3–5 (

FND-02.title: Deposits, Loans and Funding
FND-02.one_screen: Deposits and loans are easiest to understand as opposite claims viewed from opposite sides of the same contracts. Deposits are normally bank liabilities, loans made by the bank are normally bank assets, and **funding** describes the liabilities and equity that support the asset side over time.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting*, revised March 2018, Chapter 4 (
Bank of England, McLeay, Radia and Thomas, *Money creation in the modern economy*, Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1, published 14 March 2014 (

FND-03.title: How Bank Lending Creates Deposits
FND-03.one_screen: When a bank originates a loan and credits the borrower's account, it can create a loan asset and a deposit liability at the same moment. “Loans create deposits” describes that balance-sheet mechanism; it does **not** mean lending is unconstrained by funding, settlement liquidity, capital, risk, or profitability.

sources.label: Bank of England, McLeay, Radia and Thomas, *Money creation in the modern economy*, Quarterly Bulletin 2014 Q1, published 14 March 2014 (
Bank of England, *How is money created?*, last updated 1 October 2019 (

FND-04.title: The Bank Earnings Engine
FND-04.one_screen: A traditional bank earns interest on many assets and pays interest on much of its funding. **Net interest income (NII) = interest income − interest expense**; profit then reflects non-interest income, operating costs, credit-loss charges, market or valuation effects where applicable, and tax.

FND-05.title: Capital, Liquidity and Solvency
FND-05.one_screen: Capital, liquidity, and solvency answer different questions. **Capital absorbs losses; liquidity enables payments when due; solvency concerns whether the value of assets is sufficient relative to obligations.** Confusing them hides the two distinct ways a bank can fail: loss of value and loss of payment capacity.

FND-06.title: The Financial Statements and How They Link
FND-06.one_screen: Financial statements separate **position**, **performance**, **cash movement**, and **equity movement**. Profit can change equity without matching cash, financing can change cash without creating profit, and every recognised closing position ultimately appears in the closing balance sheet.

FND-07.title: Accrual Versus Cash
FND-07.one_screen: Accrual accounting records the economic effects of events when the applicable recognition requirements are met, which can be earlier or later than cash settlement. The foundational discipline is simple: **recognition timing and cash timing are different dimensions.**

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting*, revised March 2018, Chapters 3–5.
IFRS Foundation, *IAS 7 Statement of Cash Flows*, current standard through 31 August 2026.

FND-08.title: Credit-Loss Allowances and Provisions
FND-08.one_screen: Credit-loss accounting and prudential provisioning recognise that contractual claims may not be fully collected, but they are **not one universal calculation**. Recognition trigger, horizon, measurement, terminology, and prudential interaction come from the governing framework.

FND-09.title: Profit, OCI and Equity
FND-09.one_screen: Recognised gains and losses do not all have to travel through current profit or loss. Accounting frameworks can require specified items to be presented in **other comprehensive income (OCI)** or another reserve route, but that route exists because the governing framework prescribes it—not because management prefers less earnings volatility.

FND-10.title: How to Read a Bank Balance Sheet
FND-10.one_screen: A bank balance sheet should be read as a funded risk position, not as a list of totals. The efficient sequence is **assets → funding → loss absorption → quality → maturity → concentration**, because each step asks what the preceding number actually means.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting*, revised March 2018.

FND-11.title: Present Value and Discount Factors
FND-11.one_screen: Present value puts cash flows occurring at different dates onto one valuation date. A **discount factor** is the multiplier that translates a future amount backward through time; the mathematics changes value for timing, not for whether the cash flow will occur.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, application guidance on effective interest and discounting; cited only as an applied use of universal present-value mathematics.

FND-12.title: Compounding, Rates and Timing Conventions
FND-12.one_screen: Compounding moves value forward; discounting moves it backward. The formulas are simple, but financial models fail when the **rate frequency, compounding convention, cash-flow dates, and period count are inconsistent**.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A and application guidance on the effective interest method; cited as an applied financial use of rate and timing consistency.

FND-13.title: Effective Interest Rate
FND-13.one_screen: The effective interest rate (EIR) is the single rate that makes the present value of a specified future cash-flow stream equal to a specified carrying amount or price. It compresses amount, timing, interest, and qualifying fees or costs into one internally consistent yield **for the cash-flow definition being used**.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A, definitions of effective interest rate and effective interest method.

FND-14.title: NPV and Discounted Cash Shortfalls
FND-14.one_screen: Net present value (NPV) aggregates dated amounts only after translating them to one valuation date. When a loss methodology discounts expected cash shortfalls, **probability determines how much is expected; discounting determines what the timing of that expected amount is worth today.**

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, paragraph B5.5.44 and related application guidance.

FND-15.title: Probability and Expected Value
FND-15.one_screen: Probability describes likelihood; expected value converts a set of possible numerical outcomes into their probability-weighted average. An expected value is a property of a modelled distribution—not a promise that the next realised outcome will equal that average.

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods*, probability and statistical foundations

FND-16.title: Variance, Standard Deviation and Volatility
FND-16.one_screen: Expected value describes the centre of a distribution; variance describes how dispersed outcomes are around that centre. Standard deviation is the square root of variance, and in finance **volatility** usually refers to a standard-deviation measure whose meaning depends on the variable, observation frequency, and horizon.

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Measures of Scale*, section 1.3.5.6 (

FND-17.title: Quantiles and Tail Risk
FND-17.one_screen: A quantile is a threshold in a distribution associated with a cumulative probability. Tail risk concerns the outcomes beyond an extreme threshold, so a high quantile can locate the edge of a tail without telling you how severe the tail becomes.

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods*, percentile and distributional-shape material

FND-18.title: Exposure: What Is Actually at Risk
FND-18.one_screen: Exposure is the amount or position subject to adverse change from a specified risk event; it is **not the loss itself**. For credit, today's drawn balance can be only part of what is at risk because a facility may also contain undrawn commitments that can become exposure before the relevant event.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework — CRE20 Standardised approach: individual exposures*, current framework, off-balance-sheet treatment; cited only to evidence that undrawn commitments can be converted into credit exposure under a defined methodology.

FND-19.title: Expected Loss Versus Unexpected Loss
FND-19.one_screen: Expected loss is the probability-weighted average loss at the centre of a modelled loss distribution; unexpected loss is the adverse variation around that expectation for which additional resilience may be needed. A low average loss can coexist with a dangerous tail.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework — CRE30 IRB approach: overview and asset class definitions*, paragraph 30.2, and *CRE31 IRB approach: risk weight functions*, paragraph 31.1, describing separate EL and UL treatment.

FND-20.title: Risk Capacity, Appetite, Limits and Profile
FND-20.one_screen: Risk governance turns resilience into choices. **Risk capacity** is how much risk the institution can bear; **risk appetite** is how much and what types it chooses to take within that capacity; **limits** translate appetite into operating boundaries; **risk profile** is the risk actually being run.

sources.label: Financial Stability Board, *Principles for an Effective Risk Appetite Framework*, 18 November 2013.

FND-21.title: The Three Lines Model
FND-21.one_screen: The Three Lines Model separates **management's action and ownership of risk**, specialist management support and challenge, and **independent internal-audit assurance**. It is a model of roles and accountability, not a rigid organisation chart and not permission for one line to outsource responsibility to another.

FND-22.title: Policy, Standard, Procedure and Evidence
FND-22.one_screen: A useful internal-governance hierarchy is **policy → standard → procedure → evidence**: intent and mandatory outcomes become testable requirements, then execution steps, then proof that the steps occurred. The labels are not legally universal, so authority, scope, approval, and content matter more than the filename.

FND-23.title: What Regulators and Supervisors Actually Do
FND-23.one_screen: **Regulation sets applicable requirements; supervision tests institutions against those requirements and supervisory objectives.** Authorisation, reporting, examination, remediation, and enforcement surround that core according to each authority's legal mandate.

FND-24.one_screen: Prudential, conduct, and accounting frameworks can govern the same bank because they answer different questions. Their outputs interact; compliance in one never proves compliance in another.

IMP-01.one_screen: Impairment recognises that a financial asset is not expected to deliver all contractual value. The loss allowance measures expected non-collection; it changes accounting measurement without, by itself, changing what the borrower legally owes.

IMP-02.one_screen: IFRS 9, US CECL and RBI provisioning answer the same economic question—how much credit loss should be recognised now—but they do not use the same recognition architecture. Learn the framework before learning the calculation.

IMP-03.title: Scope and Financial-Statement Presentation
IMP-03.one_screen: Before measuring ECL, determine whether the instrument is inside the impairment model and where the allowance is presented. The same expected-loss idea can appear as a deduction from an asset, an OCI amount or a separate provision depending on the instrument.

IMP-04.title: Credit Loss as a Discounted Cash Shortfall
IMP-04.one_screen: Under IFRS 9, the accounting target is the present value of contractual cash that will not be collected, including loss caused by delayed collection. PD, LGD and EAD are ways to estimate that target; they are not its definition.

IMP-05.title: The IFRS 9 Three-Stage Architecture
IMP-05.one_screen: IFRS 9 changes the loss horizon as credit risk changes. Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, Stage 2 carries lifetime ECL after significant deterioration, and Stage 3 carries lifetime ECL once the asset is credit-impaired.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, Section 5.5, 24 July 2014.

IMP-06.title: Twelve-Month ECL versus Lifetime ECL
IMP-06.one_screen: Twelve-month ECL is not twelve months of cash loss. It is the lifetime loss consequence of default events that are possible within the next twelve months; lifetime ECL instead considers defaults possible over the relevant remaining life.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, paragraph B5.5.43 and Section 5.5, 24 July 2014.

IMP-07.title: Significant Increase in Credit Risk
IMP-07.one_screen: SICR asks whether the risk of default has increased significantly since initial recognition. It is therefore principally a relative deterioration test, not a test of whether current risk has crossed one universal “bad borrower” threshold.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, paragraphs 5.5.9–5.5.11 and related application guidance, 24 July 2014.

IMP-08.title: SICR Evidence, Backstops and Collective Assessment
IMP-08.one_screen: SICR must use reasonable and supportable information that becomes available before default. Delinquency is one signal; the more-than-30-DPD rule is a rebuttable backstop, while collective assessment catches deterioration that individual borrower data has not yet revealed.

IMP-09.title: Credit-Impaired Assets, Stage 3 and Interest
IMP-09.one_screen: Stage 3 means events have occurred that detrimentally affect expected future cash flows. It is more than elevated risk: lifetime ECL continues, and for assets that became credit-impaired after origination IFRS 9 also changes the base on which interest revenue is calculated.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, Appendix A and paragraph 5.4.1, 24 July 2014.

IMP-10.title: Purchased or Originated Credit-Impaired Assets
IMP-10.one_screen: A purchased or originated credit-impaired asset is already credit-impaired when first recognised. IFRS 9 therefore does not treat its initial expected loss as ordinary post-origination deterioration: the starting economics already incorporate impaired expected cash flows.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, Appendix A and paragraphs 5.4.1, 5.5.13–5.5.14, 24 July 2014.

IMP-11.title: The ECL Engine: Period-by-Period Expected Loss
IMP-11.one_screen: A common ECL engine decomposes expected loss into default timing, exposure at that time, loss severity and discounting. The decomposition is useful only if its aggregate output remains consistent with the governing expected-cash-shortfall objective.

IMP-12.title: PD Term Structures
IMP-12.one_screen: Lifetime ECL needs default risk distributed through time, not one undated lifetime percentage. Cumulative PD tells whether default has occurred by a horizon; marginal PD allocates that risk to one future interval; conditional PD measures default during that interval given survival to its start.

IMP-13.title: EAD Paths, Commitments and Revolving Life
IMP-13.one_screen: EAD is exposure at the future point of default, not today’s balance repeated through time. Amortisation, prepayment, redraws and commitments create an exposure path; revolving products can also make effective credit exposure outlive a simple contractual notice period.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, IFRS 9, paragraphs 5.5.19–5.5.20 and related application guidance, 24 July 2014.

IMP-14.title: LGD, Recoveries and Collateral
IMP-14.one_screen: LGD translates default into loss severity. For accounting ECL it must represent expected discounted shortfall after relevant borrower payments, collateral or guarantee recoveries and workout costs; a prudential-capital LGD may be calibrated to a different objective.

IMP-15.title: Forward-Looking Information and Scenarios
IMP-15.one_screen: Expected loss must respond to relevant future conditions, not only historical averages. Forward-looking information changes ECL through defensible links to default, exposure, recovery or staging, and probability weighting must capture material non-linearity rather than merely selecting one “most likely” macro path.

IMP-16.title: Overlays and Management Judgement
IMP-16.one_screen: An overlay or post-model adjustment addresses material credit risk the core model does not capture adequately. It is a controlled correction for a named limitation, not a reserve used to move the allowance toward a preferred number.

IMP-17.title: Validation, Backtesting and Staging Challenge
IMP-17.one_screen: Validation asks whether ECL is conceptually sound, correctly implemented and performing appropriately. Backtesting is one component; staging needs separate challenge because a good PD model can still produce late lifetime-loss recognition.

IMP-18.title: Allowance Movements and ECL Disclosures
IMP-18.one_screen: The closing allowance is not one opaque model output: it is the result of new business, repayments, stage migration, changed risk expectations, write-offs and other movements through the period. Disclosure makes those movements and the major judgements behind them observable.

IMP-19.title: US CECL under ASC 326
IMP-19.one_screen: CECL is a forward-looking expected-loss model, but its architecture is not IFRS 9 staging. For in-scope financial assets measured at amortised cost, lifetime expected credit losses are generally recognised from initial recognition and re-estimated each reporting date.

IMP-20.title: India: Parallel Regimes and the 2027 Bank ECL Transition
IMP-20.one_screen: India has parallel regimes. At 31 August 2026, banks remain under RBI IRACP through 31 March 2027; applicable NBFCs/ARCs use Ind AS with RBI safeguards; banks move to RBI’s staged-ECL framework on 1 April 2027.

IND-01.title: RBI's Lending Mandate and Regulatory Perimeter
IND-01.one_screen: RBI regulates Indian lending through a mix of prudential, conduct and developmental mandates. For a lender, the first question is not only "what risk rule applies?" but also "what type of regulated entity am I, what lending permissions do I have, and what directed-credit or customer-protection obligations attach to me?"

IND-02.title: Indian Lending Entity Taxonomy
IND-02.one_screen: India uses several regulated entity classes that look similar from a customer's perspective but have different lending permissions and supervisory treatment. The useful taxonomy is therefore functional: who may lend, who may accept deposits, and which RBI rulebook governs the exposure.

IND-03.title: Bank versus NBFC: The Lending Boundary
IND-03.one_screen: Banks and NBFCs can both make loans, but they are not interchangeable regulated objects. The decisive differences are banking powers, funding structure, access to the payment system and the prudential rulebook applied to the resulting credit exposure.

IND-04.title: NBFC Scale-Based Regulation
IND-04.one_screen: Scale-Based Regulation, or SBR, makes "NBFC" only the starting label. RBI places NBFCs into Base, Middle, Upper and potentially Top layers so that regulatory intensity increases with size, activity, interconnectedness and systemic significance.

IND-05.title: Housing Finance Companies under RBI
IND-05.one_screen: Housing Finance Companies are RBI-regulated non-bank lenders with a housing-finance business focus. The key teaching point is not the historical transfer from NHB itself, but the current position: HFCs sit inside RBI's NBFC regulatory estate while retaining HFC-specific business and prudential requirements.

IND-06.title: Priority Sector Lending: Obligation and Applicability
IND-06.one_screen: Priority Sector Lending, or PSL, converts RBI's developmental mandate into measurable lending obligations. It answers two questions before any category test begins: which lender is subject to PSL, and what overall target framework applies to that lender.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Priority Sector Lending - Targets and Classification Directions, 2025, RBI/FIDD/2024-25/128, 24 March 2025.

IND-07.title: Priority Sector Eligibility and Classification
IND-07.one_screen: PSL is not a label a lender can attach to any socially useful loan. An exposure counts only when it satisfies the RBI definition for an eligible category, including borrower, purpose, size or activity conditions where the current Directions prescribe them.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Priority Sector Lending - Targets and Classification Directions, 2025, RBI/FIDD/2024-25/128, 24 March 2025.

IND-08.title: PSL Achievement, PSLCs and Shortfalls
IND-08.one_screen: A bank can meet PSL through qualifying assets on its own book and, where permitted, through the Priority Sector Lending Certificate market. PSLCs move regulatory achievement between banks without transferring the underlying loan, so credit risk and PSL compliance must be kept conceptually separate.

IND-09.title: Fair Lending: KFS, APR, Charges and Disclosure
IND-09.one_screen: Indian lending conduct rules increasingly force price and key contractual terms into a standard pre-contract disclosure. The Key Facts Statement, or KFS, is the central customer-facing object: it makes the annual percentage rate and material charges visible before the borrower is bound.

IND-10.title: Lending Rates: Benchmark, Spread, Reset and Prepayment
IND-10.one_screen: RBI does not prescribe one universal lending-rate formula for every Indian loan. Rate governance depends on lender and product, but the recurring structure is benchmark plus contractual spread, with rules on reset, borrower communication and, for specified floating-rate loans, prepayment treatment.

IND-11.title: Digital Lending Perimeter: RE, LSP and DLA
IND-11.one_screen: Digital lending changes the channel, not the identity of the regulated creditor. RBI separates the Regulated Entity that owns the loan, the Lending Service Provider that performs outsourced functions, and the Digital Lending App through which the customer may interact.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025, RBI/2025-26/36, DOR.STR.REC.19/21.07.001/2025-26, 8 May 2025.

IND-12.title: Digital Lending Transaction and Customer Controls
IND-12.one_screen: RBI's digital-lending rules control the customer journey as well as the lender's legal perimeter. The core idea is traceability: the borrower should know the regulated lender, understand the price, consent to data use, and have funds and repayments move through permitted channels.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025, RBI/2025-26/36, DOR.STR.REC.19/21.07.001/2025-26, 8 May 2025.

IND-13.title: Default Loss Guarantee
IND-13.one_screen: RBI's current term is Default Loss Guarantee, or DLG. A DLG is credit support provided to a regulated lender against losses on a fixed, identifiable loan portfolio; it does not turn the guarantor into the lender and it does not delay NPA recognition.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025, RBI/2025-26/36, DOR.STR.REC.19/21.07.001/2025-26, 8 May 2025.

IND-14.title: Co-Lending Arrangements: Structure and Risk Retention
IND-14.one_screen: RBI's 2025 Co-Lending Arrangements Directions govern joint lending by eligible regulated entities to a common borrower. The defining idea is genuine shared exposure: each participating RE must hold an agreed portion of every loan and retain at least the prescribed minimum share.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India (Co-Lending Arrangements) Directions, 2025, RBI/DOR/2025-26/139, DOR.STR.REC.44/13.07.010/2025-26, 6 August 2025, effective 1 January 2026.

IND-15.title: Co-Lending Operations and Classification Synchronisation
IND-15.one_screen: The hardest part of co-lending is operational consistency across two regulated balance sheets. Each RE books only its share, but the borrower experience, servicing data, credit-information reporting and stress classification must be coordinated so that one common loan does not become two contradictory regulatory stories.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Reserve Bank of India (Co-Lending Arrangements) Directions, 2025, RBI/DOR/2025-26/139, DOR.STR.REC.44/13.07.010/2025-26, 6 August 2025, effective 1 January 2026.

IND-16.title: Account Aggregator Consent Architecture
IND-16.one_screen: The Account Aggregator, or AA, framework lets a customer move financial information between regulated participants through a standard consent architecture. The AA is neither the lender nor the data owner: it manages permissioned transmission between a Financial Information Provider and a Financial Information User.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, Master Direction - Non-Banking Financial Company - Account Aggregator, 2016, as amended.

IND-17.title: Lending Data Rails: GSTN, ULI and the OCEN Boundary
IND-17.one_screen: India's lending stack increasingly separates data access from credit decisioning. GST and other public or financial data can feed underwriting through consented or authorised rails, while the Unified Lending Interface, or ULI, standardises access to multiple data sources; OCEN is best treated as adjacent open credit-enablement infrastructure, not as an RBI-regulated lender.

IND-18.title: Credit Information Ecosystem: CIC, CIR and Bureau Score
IND-18.one_screen: India's Credit Information Companies, or CICs, collect regulated credit information from lenders and return Credit Information Reports and related scores. A bureau score is a proprietary risk signal derived from reported history; it is not an RBI approval threshold and it does not replace underwriting.

IND-19.title: Credit Information Reporting and Correction Cycle
IND-19.one_screen: Credit-information regulation is operational: lenders must submit accurate borrower data, CICs must process it, and customers need a route to challenge errors. The value of the bureau system depends on update discipline because stale arrears, closed loans or incorrect balances can distort subsequent lending decisions.

IND-20.title: IRACP: India's Prudential Asset-Quality Regime
IND-20.one_screen: IRACP is India's prudential regime for Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning on advances. It answers whether a loan is performing or non-performing for RBI purposes, what income may be recognised and what minimum prudential provision is required; it is distinct from Ind AS 109 ECL.

IND-21.title: Special Mention Accounts
IND-21.one_screen: Special Mention Accounts, or SMAs, are RBI's pre-NPA stress buckets for specified credit exposures. They create a disciplined early-warning ladder before the standard 90-day NPA threshold, and the legacy pack's 31-60, 61-90 and 91-180 day sequence is incorrect.

IND-22.title: NPA Recognition, Income Recognition and Asset Classes
IND-22.one_screen: An NPA is a prudential status, not merely an internal "bad loan" label. Once the applicable RBI trigger is met, income recognition changes and the exposure moves through sub-standard, doubtful and loss categories according to the current entity-specific IRACP rules.

IND-27.one_screen: Compromise settlement and technical write-off are different exit tools. A compromise changes the amount or terms the creditor agrees to accept in full or partial settlement; a technical write-off removes an exposure from the active books while legal recovery rights can continue.

IND-28.one_screen: SARFAESI gives eligible secured creditors a statutory route to enforce qualifying security interests without first obtaining an ordinary civil-court decree, while Debt Recovery Tribunals provide a specialised adjudicatory and recovery forum. MRM-01.title: What Counts as a Model
MRM-01.one_screen: A model is a governed representation that transforms inputs into outputs using assumptions and quantitative or cognitive techniques. Classification is consequential: model status brings inventory, validation, approval, monitoring and change controls, while the legal boundary differs materially across jurisdictions.

MRM-02.title: Model Risk as a Distinct Risk Type
MRM-02.one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse consequences from relying on a model whose design, data, implementation, limitations or use make its output unreliable for the decision being taken. It is distinct from the underlying risk being measured: the borrower can be unchanged while a credit model is wrong, and the market can be unchanged while a valuation model is wrong.

MRM-03.title: Where Model Risk Comes From
MRM-03.one_screen: Model risk is rarely one defect called "bad modelling". It can enter through data, assumptions, methodology, implementation, use or environmental change, and the same bad output can require a completely different remedy depending on which source failed.

MRM-04.one_screen: There is no single global legal perimeter for MRM. The US uses broad, tailored supervisory guidance; the PRA applies SS1/23 to specified firms but across their model types; the EU prudential regime focuses on approved internal models; and India's proposed 2026 framework is broader but remains draft as at August 2026.

MRM-05.one_screen: The model inventory is the authoritative record of what models exist, where they are in the lifecycle, who owns and uses them, and which other systems or models they depend on. A mere list of names is insufficient: the control value comes from linking identity, status, use, lineage, dependencies and governance state.

MRM-06.title: Materiality and Risk Tiering
MRM-06.one_screen: Tiering converts model characteristics and business impact into proportional control intensity. The purpose is not to declare low-tier models harmless; it is to spend validation, approval, monitoring and governance effort where model failure can matter most while preserving a minimum control floor for every governed model.

MRM-07.title: Aggregate Model Risk and Risk Appetite
MRM-07.one_screen: Managing models one by one can miss the largest exposure: several individually acceptable models may rely on the same data, assumptions, vendor or economic relationship and fail together. Aggregate model risk therefore combines model-level risk with concentration and dependency, then compares that enterprise exposure with the institution's model risk appetite and tolerance.

MRM-08.title: The Model Lifecycle and Its Control Gates
MRM-08.one_screen: A model lifecycle is not a project plan; it is a sequence of governed states in which evidence must be sufficient before the model can move forward. The key control idea is the gate: development does not grant use, validation does not grant approval, approval does not end monitoring, and change can reopen earlier gates.

MRM-09.title: Who Produces, Uses, Approves, Challenges and Audits
MRM-09.one_screen: Ownership is the load-bearing control in MRM because the same person should not create evidence, decide whether that evidence is convincing, accept the residual risk and audit the process. Effective governance separates production, consumption, approval, independent challenge and assurance while ensuring the challenger has expertise, standing and access to decision-makers.

MRM-10.title: Purpose, Intended Use and Limitations
MRM-10.one_screen: Development begins by fixing the decision the model is supposed to support, the population and conditions it covers, and the limitations users must respect. Without that mandate, developers cannot choose evidence coherently and validators cannot decide whether "good performance" is relevant to the actual use.

MRM-11.title: Data Lineage and Fitness for Use
MRM-11.one_screen: Model data is not sound merely because it is clean. It must be traceable from source to model, correctly transformed, sufficiently complete, representative of the intended use and governed consistently between development and production; a perfectly coded model trained or run on unsuitable data remains unreliable.

MRM-12.title: Method, Assumptions and Complexity
MRM-12.one_screen: Method selection is a governed judgement about whether the model structure, assumptions and complexity are appropriate for the stated purpose and available data. MRM does not own the derivation of statistical methods; it owns the evidence that the chosen method is defensible, its assumptions are visible, and added complexity earns its place.

MRM-13.title: Implementation, Versioning and Reproducibility
MRM-13.one_screen: A validated methodology is useless if production executes something different. Implementation control proves that approved logic, data transformations, parameters, dependencies and configuration are faithfully reproduced, while versioning and reproducibility make it possible to determine exactly which model generated a past output.
